prize_parts.citation: For the discovery that biomolecular phase separation organizes the interior of living cells into membraneless compartments.

statement.case_for: Biomolecular phase separation is a new concept of molecular organisation: demixing, multivalency, interfacial tension and viscoelasticity applied to proteins and nucleic acids inside cells. Brangwynne and Hyman showed that P granules behave as liquids, and Rosen showed with defined multivalent proteins that a sharp phase transition can be reconstituted in vitro and tuned by valency and affinity. The concept has been taken up in cell biology, neurodegeneration and drug discovery, and more than a decade of work gives it a record that can be assessed. Its roots are in physical chemistry, which is the kind of discovery the chemistry prize has not recognised often.
statement.case_against: Which cellular condensates are truly phase-separated, as opposed to artefacts of overexpression or loosely labelled assemblies, is still contested, and the label is sometimes applied without quantitative phase-diagram evidence. The three-person limit excludes Pappu and Mittag, who supplied the sequence grammar and the physical theory. A reasonable colleague could say that it belongs to physiology or medicine more than to chemistry, or that it is a few years early. Candidates with a settled mechanism and a clear clinical or practical record, such as B034 and B066, face less of this risk.

responses.point: Daniel ranks condensates third, praising the conceptual reach but saying the mechanistic chemistry is less tightly defined than for a discrete invention, and that the work may be premature for Chemistry.
responses.response: I accept that condensates are less of a discrete molecular invention than B041 or B034, but I think this is a point in their favour for Chemistry: the contribution is a physical-chemical principle, not a reagent. Rosen's in vitro work defines it quantitatively, through valency, affinity and phase boundaries, so the chemistry is tighter than the in vivo literature suggests. I agree prematurity is a real risk and I would want the citation worded around the principle, not around any specific cellular body.

responses.point: Andrei ranks B052 fourth and wants stricter quantitative validation, citing overexpression artefacts and doubts about whether condensates have functional roles.
responses.response: This is the strongest objection, and I share part of it: many in vivo claims do not show a phase boundary or a concentration threshold at endogenous expression. My answer is that the prize would honour the founding demonstrations, namely P-granule liquid behaviour and reconstituted multivalent phase transitions, and these have held up under independent quantitative tests. It would not honour every use of the word condensate. If he can name a specific control that the founding work fails, I would reconsider; otherwise I think the overreach of the later literature does not count against the origin.

responses.point: Johan ranks B023 first and puts B052 eighth, saying the concept is still debated in generality and mechanism, that Rosen, Pappu and Mittag are all essential, and that the chemistry versus biology placement is uncertain.
responses.response: I take the attribution point seriously and I do not think a three-person cut is clean. But the same is true of his own first choice, where Kosugi's precedent is a priority question, and his top candidate B023 is a well-known and well-settled method that follows a 2010 prize on a closely related theme. I do not see novelty of concept in B023 on the scale of B052. On debate over generality, thermodynamics gives a standard of proof, and the best-characterised systems meet it.

responses.point: Heiner ranks nanopores first and condensates seventh, finding the thermodynamic framing compelling but saying the principle is widely adopted with debate over physiological relevance and over-use of the label.
responses.response: I agree with his reading of the physics and with the risk that the label is over-used. Where I differ is on how much weight that carries: the nanopore case rests on a mature, clearly proven device, and I rank it sixth, so we differ more in degree than in kind. My question to him is whether he sees a way to protect the prize from over-use of the term, since I think a citation focused on the principle and on liquid behaviour of defined biomolecules does this.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the founding demonstrations stand independently of the unresolved in vivo controversy
Whether leaving out Pappu and Mittag is acceptable, or whether a two-part prize would handle it better, which the three-person limit makes hard
Whether B052 will be seen as Chemistry and not Physiology or Medicine
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. I work in lipid and membrane physical chemistry and share a department tradition with Heiner Linke and Peter Somfai at Lund, but I have no stated personal or institutional tie to any shortlisted candidate. My field is close to B066 (lipid nanoparticles) and to B052, so I note it for transparency.
